question: What is a Type II error and what is statistical power?
answer: A Type II error is failing to reject a false null hypothesis, with probability beta [S1]. Statistical power is 1 - beta, the probability of detecting a real effect [S1].

citations.title: Statistics Lecture Notes
citations.text: 5. Hypothesis Testing Hypothesis testing evaluates a claim about a population. The null hypothesis H0 states no effect or no difference; the alternative hypothesis H1 states the effect we are looking for. We compute a test statistic from the sample and a p-value, the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one found, assuming H0 is true. If the p-value is smaller than the significance level alpha, commonly 0.05, we reject H0. A Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis, and its probability is alpha. A Type II error means failing to reject a false null hypothesis, with probability beta. Power equals 1 - beta, the probability of detecting a real effect. Larger samples increase power. A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and a small p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect.

S2.title: Python Lecture Notes
S2.text: 1. Variables and Data Types A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory. In Python you create a variable by assignment, for example age = 21. Python is dynamically typed: the type belongs to the value, not to the name, so the same name can later refer to a string. The core built-in types are int (whole numbers), float (decimal numbers), str (text), bool (True or False) and NoneType (the single value None, meaning "no value"). The function type(x) reports the type of x. Conversion functions such as int("42"), float("3.5") and str(10) create new values of another type; int("abc") raises a ValueError. Strings are immutable sequences of characters. Indexing starts at zero, so "python"[0] is "p", and negative indexes count from the end, so "python"[-1] is "n". Slicing "python"[1:4] returns "yth" (start included, stop excluded).

S3.title: Python Reference Notes
S3.text:
COMMON ERRORS AND THEIR MEANING
SyntaxError: the code is not valid Python, for example a missing colon after if.
IndentationError: the indentation of a block is inconsistent.
NameError: a variable or function name was used before it was defined.
TypeError: an operation was applied to the wrong type, such as "a" + 1.
ValueError: the type is right but the value is not, such as int("abc").
KeyError: a dictionary key does not exist.
IndexError: a list index is outside the valid range.
ZeroDivisionError: division or modulo by zero.
FileNotFoundError: the file path does not exist.

S4.title: Statistics Exercise Guide
S4.text:
Problem 3: Confidence Interval for a Mean
Question. A sample of n = 36 students has mean study time 12.4 hours per week. The population standard deviation is known to be 3 hours. Build a 95% confidence interval.
Solution. The standard error is 3 / sqrt(36) = 0.5. The margin of error is 1.96 * 0.5 = 0.98. The interval is 12.4 plus or minus 0.98, that is (11.42, 13.38). Interpretation: the procedure captures the true mean in about 95% of repeated samples. If the sample size were four times larger (n = 144) the standard error would halve to 0.25 and the interval would become narrower.

S5.title: Statistics Reference Notes
S5.text:
INFERENCE
95% confidence interval for a mean (sigma known): x-bar +/- 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n)
t statistic: t = (x-bar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n)), with n - 1 degrees of freedom
Type I error rate = alpha. Power = 1 - beta.
Chi-square statistic: sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected)

S6.title: Python Glossary Overloaded Terms
S6.text: class: in Python a class is a blueprint for creating objects. It is not a category label as in classification problems. function: a reusable block of code defined with def. It is not necessarily a mathematical function. mode: when opening a file the mode string such as "r", "w" or "a" says how the file is used. statistics.mode(data) is a different thing: it returns the most frequent value. sample: random.sample(population, k) draws k unique elements without replacement. It has nothing to do with a statistical sample unless you use it to build one. normal: random.gauss(mu, sigma) and random.normalvariate(mu, sigma) draw numbers from a normal distribution. seed: random.seed(n) makes the random sequence reproducible, so a program prints the same random numbers on every run. iterable: an object you can loop over, such as a list or string.

S7.title: Statistics Exercise Guide
S7.text:
Problem 4: One-Sample Hypothesis Test
Question. A factory claims bulbs last 1000 hours on average. A sample of 25 bulbs has mean 980 and sample standard deviation 50. Test H0: mu = 1000 against H1: mu is not 1000 at alpha = 0.05.
Solution. The t statistic is (980 - 1000) / (50 / sqrt(25)) = -20 / 10 = -2.0 with 24 degrees of freedom. The two-sided critical value is about 2.064. Because the absolute value 2.0 is smaller than 2.064 we fail to reject H0 at the 5% level. Failing to reject does not prove the claim is true; the sample may simply lack the power to detect a 20 hour difference.
